introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2025. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry TWENTY-FIVE marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Question 4(c)(i) et (ii) regroupées dans la sous-question « c » (6 + 4 = 10 marks imprimés). Chiffres démographiques donnés en ordres de grandeur (population mondiale d'environ 8 milliards, croissance du Cameroun d'environ 2,5 % par an, politique de l'enfant unique en Chine de 1980 à 2015). Quartiers de banlieue cités (Soa, Mbankomo, Yassa, Logbessou) comme exemples plausibles de navetteurs, à faire relire.

Page de garde vérifiée : JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography, Paper 2, code 0750, durée Three Hours. Sujet scanné de quatre pages (page de garde, deux pages de questions, une page de fond de carte). Filigranes et bandeaux gcerevision.com ignorés.

Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section » (Section A : questions 1 à 3 ; Section B : questions 4 à 6 ; Section C : question 7 seule, en deux versions EITHER / OR). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé par section (`parmi 1 sur 3` pour A et B, `parmi 1 sur 1` pour C) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. La question 7 est codée « a », « b » (EITHER) et « OR-a », « OR-b », « OR-c » (OR), reliées par une règle `ou`.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans source consultable. Les exemples cités (lieux, programmes, accords, institutions) sont des exemples reconnus ; les chiffres sont des ordres de grandeur. Faits à faire relire par un géographe avant mise en avant. Points : chaque question est imprimée à 25 marks et les sous-parties somment à 25 (Q1 5+6+6+8 ; Q2 8+8+9, la sous-question (a) n'ayant aucun mark imprimé ; Q3 8+9+8 ; Q4 7+8+6+4 ; Q5 6+9+5+5 ; Q6 8+8+9 ; Q7 EITHER 8+8+9, OR 9+8+8). Aucun écart avec le sujet.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) How has rapid population growth become a contemporary challenge, and what can be done to mitigate the situation?

(7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Rapid population growth.** The population of the world has grown from about 2.5 billion in 1950 to about 8 billion today. The fastest growth is in the developing countries (in sub-Saharan Africa, including Cameroon, where the population is growing at roughly 2.5 per cent a year), because **birth rates remain high (high fertility) while death rates have fallen** thanks to better medicine, vaccination, water supply and food (the second stage of the **demographic transition**). The population doubles in about 25 to 30 years at such rates.

**Why it has become a contemporary challenge (any four points).**

1. **Pressure on resources:** food (shortages, malnutrition, food insecurity), fresh water, farmland and energy do not grow as fast as the population; fragmentation of land holdings.
2. **Unemployment and underemployment:** too many young people (a young population structure with a high dependency ratio) compete for few jobs, which leads to poverty, crime and emigration.
3. **Pressure on social services and housing:** schools, hospitals, housing and sanitation are overcrowded and underfunded; slums and informal settlements grow.
4. **Rural-urban migration and urban problems:** congestion, pollution, insecurity and waste in the large cities.
5. **Environmental damage:** deforestation, soil exhaustion and erosion, overgrazing, pollution and loss of biodiversity.
6. **Economic effects:** the economic growth is absorbed by the increase in population, so the income per person stays low and savings and investment are small.

**What can be done to mitigate the situation (any three points).**

1. **Family planning and health care:** make contraception and birth spacing available, and lower the infant mortality (parents who are sure that their children will survive have fewer).
2. **Education, especially of girls and the empowerment of women:** educated women marry later, have fewer children and take part in the work force; also laws on the minimum age of marriage.
3. **Government population policies:** sensitisation, and incentives or penalties (such as the one-child policy of China from 1980 until 2015, or the family planning programme of India and of Thailand and Iran).
4. **Economic development and job creation:** investment in industry and agriculture (using the Green Revolution methods) and technology to increase the food and jobs; improved income lowers fertility.
5. **Redistribution and emigration:** resettlement schemes and rural development to avoid overcrowding of the cities, and the decentralisation of the activities.

**Conclusion.** The growth of population is a challenge when it exceeds the growth of the resources; the solutions are to reduce fertility by education and health and, at the same time, to raise production and jobs.

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Explain the reasons for an inverse relationship between the volume of migration and distance travelled by migrants.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
An **inverse relationship** means that the volume of migration falls as the distance rises: most migrants move a short distance, and the further the destination, the fewer the migrants. This is the **distance decay** effect observed by Ravenstein in the "laws of migration" (1885: "the majority of migrants go only a short distance") and is expressed in the **gravity model** of migration (the movement between two places is proportional to their sizes and inversely proportional to the distance between them). In Cameroon, for example, most rural migrants go first to the nearest town (such as Bafoussam, Bamenda, Garoua or Ebolowa) and fewer reach the farthest cities, Douala and Yaounde, or other countries.

**Reasons (any four, with explanation).**

1. **The cost of the journey.** The longer the distance, the higher the transport cost, the cost of food and lodging on the way and of the establishment at the destination, and the longer the time lost; poor people, who are the majority of the migrants, can only afford short trips.
2. **Imperfect information.** People know more about the near places (through relatives, friends, markets and the radio) than the far places; the farther the destination, the less the information and the greater the uncertainty and the **risk** of failure, so fewer people dare to go.
3. **Social and family ties.** Migrants prefer to stay near their relatives, friends and their home village; they want to visit often, to send remittances and to return easily (for farming, for funerals and for festivals). Short-distance moves keep the links, the long-distance ones break them.
4. **Cultural similarities.** Nearby places share a language, customs, religion, food and way of living, so adaptation is easy; far areas can be culturally different and the migrants may be discriminated against.
5. **Intervening opportunities** (Stouffer). Migrants stop at the first suitable place that offers work or land, so fewer reach the far destinations; the nearer places are numerous.
6. **Physical and political barriers.** Mountains, rivers, poor roads, borders, visas, permits and laws increase with the distance travelled, especially for international moves, and make it difficult.
7. **Age and the type of migrant.** Long-distance migrants are mostly the young and educated, who are fewer, while short-distance migration includes women (marriage), families and the old.

**Exceptions.** Because of improved transport, communication and information (mobile phones and the internet), and the pull of big cities and developed countries, the effect of distance is decreasing; forced migrants (refugees) and skilled workers may move long distances.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) With increasing technology and affluence, it has been observed that majority of Cameroonians working in major cities like Yaounde and Douala live out of the city and commute everyday to work, using either private cars or public transport.

i) Account for this form of movement.

(6 marks)

ii) Explain **TWO** disadvantages of commuting to the community.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Reasons for this form of movement (6 marks)**

**Commuting** is the daily movement between the place of residence and the place of work. People live in the outskirts or in the towns and villages around Yaounde and Douala (for example the districts of Soa and Mbankomo near Yaounde, or Yassa and Logbessou near Douala) and travel to the city for work. The reasons are as follows (any four to six, explained).

1. **High cost and shortage of housing in the city.** Rent and the price of land and houses in the central areas are very high, and housing is scarce; the land on the periphery is cheaper and plots are larger, so many workers build or rent outside the city (and some use family land).
2. **Environmental and social conditions of the city.** Congestion, noise, air pollution, floods in the poor neighbourhoods, insecurity and crowding drive the well-off families to seek a quieter, cleaner and safer environment in the suburbs (**suburbanisation**, the desire for a better quality of life, space, gardens and fresh air).
3. **Increased affluence and car ownership.** Rising incomes allow more families to buy a house in the outskirts and to buy a car or to pay for the transport; the increased use of motorcycles, taxis and minibuses makes daily trips possible.
4. **Improved transport and technology.** Better roads, the expansion of public transport (buses, shared taxis and motorcycle taxis), electricity, water, telephone and internet in the outer areas, and mobile phones that allow people to plan journeys and to keep in contact, reduce the "friction of distance".
5. **Concentration of the jobs and services in the city.** The administration, the industry, the commerce, the banks and the best schools and hospitals are in the city centre and the main industrial areas (the CBD and the port in Douala), so that people must go there to work although they live elsewhere.
6. **Planning and housing policy.** Government and private housing estates, site-and-service schemes and urban redevelopment (demolition of the old central districts) have moved people to the peripheral estates; land speculation also pushes people out.

**(ii) Two disadvantages of commuting to the community (4 marks)**

1. **Traffic congestion, accidents and pollution.** The roads and the public transport are overloaded at the peak hours. The congestion leads to long delays, to more road accidents and to air pollution and noise from vehicles and a higher consumption of fuel, which harm the health of the inhabitants of the roads and the city.
2. **Social and economic costs to the community.** Commuters spend their time and their money in the city and so the **suburban or home community** loses their daily presence: its life is weak (a "dormitory" settlement), with less participation in community activities, less local spending, and less local development, while the city loses the revenue of the households that live outside. In addition, the long journeys cause tiredness and lost working hours, and the building of houses by the commuters consumes farmland on the outskirts and increases the pressure on the services (roads, water and electricity) and the **urban sprawl**, which the municipality has to pay for.
*(Other answers: the cost of the road maintenance and of new transport infrastructure; stress, loss of time and of family life; the rise of the cost of land that make the local inhabitants poorer.)*
